The night before, Kashish lay on the terrace floor going over it in his head. Someone will say "let's skip", it always happens on Fridays. If they do, then I say, "I have a test next period," and I walk to class. No long explaining, no arguing. He said the sentence aloud twice to the water tank, so it would come out easier than when his stomach was in knots.

At recess the next day Preeti bumped his shoulder. "Skip physics? The ground's free."

Kashish's mouth was dry, but the words were already waiting. "I've got a test next period. Catch you after." He picked up his bag and left. It was a small quiz, but a real one, and his hands only started shaking when he reached the corridor.

subtype: Approach: prepares an if-then reply to handle peer pressure [Thinking]
passage:
Dear Lokesh,
You asked how I handle the gang at the back gate who bunk the last period. Here's my secret, and it's not bravery.
Last month they asked me to come to the arcade with them during Hindi. I stood there with my mouth open, didn't know what to say, and nearly went, just because saying no felt awkward.
That night I thought about it. The problem wasn't that I wanted to go. It was that I had no words ready. So I decided: if they ask me to skip class, then I say, "I've got a test, catch you after," and walk to class. Same words every time. No explaining.
Yesterday they asked again. I said it without even thinking and walked off. Nobody even argued.
Try it. Pick your line before they ask.
Baljeet

qa.q: What line did Baljeet decide to use?
qa.a: "I've got a test, catch you after."

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel the first time the gang asked?
qa.a: Baljeet felt awkward and flustered, standing with an open mouth and nearly going along just to avoid saying no.

qa.q: Why does deciding the words beforehand help?
qa.a: Because in the moment there's no need to think or explain, so saying no feels easy instead of awkward.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Lokesh may feel encouraged and less alone, with a simple plan to try against the same pressure.

grounding: It shows a teenager planning that if friends offer to skip class, the reply is a set line about a test and walking away, which makes the words easier to say.

subtype: Approach: prepares an if-then reply to handle peer pressure [Thinking]
passage:
Kalyani, you asked on your channel how teenagers deal with peer pressure, so here's Zubin's actual method. It's boring, but it works.
In Class 11 my friends started skipping the Saturday practical and going to the lake. They'd ask right outside the lab, with everyone watching. The first two times I made up long excuses and they laughed. The third time I just went. And I hated it the whole afternoon.
So I sat down and planned it like a sum. When does it happen? Saturday, outside the lab. What do they say? "Come on, bunk." What will I say? "Can't, test prep, see you later." Then I walk in. No reasons, no debate.
The next Saturday they asked. I said my line and walked into the lab before anyone could reply. My heart was thumping, but it was easy.
Having the words ready is the whole trick.

qa.q: Where did Zubin's friends ask about skipping?
qa.a: Right outside the lab, with everyone watching.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel the afternoon at the lake?
qa.a: Zubin hated it the whole afternoon, feeling unhappy about giving in.

qa.q: What else could Zubin do if the friends keep pushing?
qa.a: Zubin could spend Saturdays with classmates who stay for practical, so there's less pressure and more support.

qa.q: How might Zubin's friends see the short reply?
qa.a: They may be surprised, but a short, calm line gives them nothing to argue with, so they let it go.

grounding: It shows a teenager preparing an if-then reply for when friends ask to skip class, which makes saying no easier.
